A four-sided frame is easily pushed out of shape (into a parallelogram), but a triangle isn't, because the lengths of its three sides already decide the shape. If the robot's arm or chassis wobbles, first look for where there's a "four-sided frame" and add a diagonal brace.
313261|Try it: build a four-sided frame with 4 beams and 4 pins and push it by hand to see whether it skews. Then add a diagonal brace and compare. Write how the two felt on a "test record" page.

When a wheel (without slipping) turns once, the robot moves one circumference. So: distance = turns × circumference; turns = distance ÷ circumference. This is the principle behind the program's "drive forward for □ mm" — VEXcode converts it using the wheel size you set.

2cb326|Try it: measure your wheel's diameter (mm) and work out the circumference. Draw a straight line on the floor, turn the wheel by hand 3 times, measure how far the robot actually goes, compare it with the calculation and note the error.

Two meshing gears turn in opposite directions. A small gear driving a big gear: slower, more force (reduction), good for an arm lifting heavy things. A big gear driving a small gear: faster, less force (speed-up). Driven turns = driving turns × driving teeth ÷ driven teeth.
8203b0|Try it: mesh a 12-tooth gear with a 36-tooth gear, turn the 12-tooth gear 3 times and count how many times the 36-tooth gear turns (it should be 1). Write the result in your notebook.

A robot with drive wheels on the left and right (differential drive): when both sides go the same direction at the same speed it goes straight; in opposite directions it turns in place; if one side is faster it arcs toward the slower side. If it drifts when you want a straight line, the two sides often have different speeds or friction.
5bd814|Try it: run "drive forward for 1000 mm", measure how far it drifted and to which side. Guess the cause, change one thing, test again and record it in a "test record".

The longer the arm, the farther the load at its tip is from the pivot (a longer lever arm), and the harder the motor has to work. To lift heavy things: shorten the arm, or use reduction gears to gain force. Use rubber on claw surfaces; more friction grips more securely.
d8ae48|Try it: hang the same weight near the pivot and then far from the pivot of an arm and compare which one can be lifted. Record it in your notebook.

Put heavy parts (battery, Brain) low and near the middle so the robot is less likely to tip over when turning, stopping suddenly or hitting something.
a56efe|Try it: mount the Brain high first and then low, push the robot at an angle by hand and see which is harder to tip.
